opening.headline: Instead of copying prompts, what is needed to have everyone on the team use AI in the same way is explained through the structure of a custom assistant.
body: The same prompts are copied and passed around in team chat rooms. Some team members only paste the first part, others use older versions, and the tone and format of the results vary from person to person. Copying and writing prompts makes it difficult to get the entire team to work in the same way.

In this class, we will look at how Claude's skills and custom assistants (GPTs, Gems), which are a bundle of instructions, knowledge, and tools, solve this problem. Next, we will distinguish the difference between project guidelines and custom assistants, check the flow of the two functions being transferred to plug-ins and skills, and follow the process of designing a customer inquiry classification assistant through the instructor's commentary.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain a custom assistant consisting of instructions, knowledge, and tools
Can tell the difference between project guidelines and custom assistants

screens.title: I want everyone on my team to use it the same way.
screens.lead: We organized in order what happened in the team chat room. When you select each item, you will see what has changed.

visual.alt: A team chat room with three copied messages with the same long prompt, with three different results below.

items.prompt: A prompt has appeared in the team chat room.
items.answer: A team member posted a well-crafted customer service prompt in the team chat room. At first everyone was welcome. However, since the prompt is written, it is separated from the original the moment you copy it.

items.prompt: Team member B only pasted the first part
items.answer: While copying a long prompt, I missed the last few lines of the rule. I didn't notice it, and the model can't follow the missing rules. You may believe you're using the same prompt, but you're actually using a different prompt.

items.prompt: Team member C is using an older version
items.answer: Although the prompt has been fixed once, team member C finds the old message and writes it as is. No one knows where the latest version is or who maintains it. Even if the rules change, there is no way to reflect this across the team.

items.prompt: Results vary from person to person
items.answer: Tone and format vary from person to person. Materials that need to be referenced are also attached to separate files. The question for this class is this. What do you need other than copying the prompts to get the whole team to use the same method?

screens.outro: First, let's think about what our team looks like.

screens.title: Think about our team’s prompt copying habits
screens.lead: Read the questions below and answer them in your head. There are no fields to enter or submit.

paragraphs: Is your team copying the same prompts? Imagine saving your favorite prompts in a document, chat room, or personal note and pasting them whenever you need them.
Who maintains the latest version of that prompt? When I change a prompt, is there a way for all team members to use the same version?

Where are the references needed to accompany the prompt, such as scope sheets or past cases? On this screen, you don't have to write down your answer, just think about it. If you can answer these questions confidently, your team already has a management structure in place.

callout.label: Organizing the instructor's thoughts
callout.text: Copying and writing prompts is convenient for individuals, but difficult to manage for teams. The starting point for custom assistants is to bundle prompts, resources, and necessary tools in one place and have your team members open and use them.

screens.outro: Let's take a look at what components that bundle consists of.

screens.title: Custom Assistant: A bundle of instructions, knowledge and tools
screens.lead: You can select the numbered markers in the picture to see what each of the components that make up your custom assistant does. Please select them in order starting from number 1.

visual.alt: The structure of a custom assistant that contains a name, description, conversation starter, instructions, knowledge, and tool slots in one large box.
labels: Same settings no matter who opens it

markers.label: Name and Description
markers.title: face visible to user
markers.body: ChatGPT help explains that the name, description, and conversation starter are what the user sees. Your name will appear at the top of search results, shared links, and chat, so it's clear what you do. The description briefly tells you the purpose, who you are talking about, and what you can do to help.

markers.label: Conversation Starter Phrases
markers.title: Examples of what to ask first
markers.body: This is an example question that appears when you open the Assistant. Include a few realistic, valuable questions that will help your team members know how to ask. It allows you to start right away without having to copy the prompt. The advantage is that there is no need to separately provide instructions on how to use it.

markers.label: instructions
markers.title: What to do and how to answer
markers.body: Guidelines dictate what your assistant should do, how it should respond, and what it should avoid. It applies to all conversations, driving tone, structure, and judgment. If it's a multi-step task, the help recommends writing down explicit steps like "If this happens, do this" and focusing on what needs to be done rather than just listing out prohibitions.

markers.label: knowledge
markers.title: Uploaded References
markers.body: Knowledge allows you to retrieve and use information from uploaded files. Ideal for reference content such as documents, guides, handbooks, and internal resources. The help tells you to use knowledge as a reference rather than as rules or actions, and to write down rules, tone, and workflow in instructions. Up to 20 files, up to 512MB each.

markers.label: tools
markers.title: Features like web search, code analysis, and external connectivity
markers.body: Functions include web search, image creation, canvas, code execution and data analysis, and connection to external apps. There are also actions that directly define and connect to external APIs. Available scope varies by account, workspace, and region. It is best to add tools only when absolutely necessary.

screens.outro: Let’s compare the creation structures of the three companies.

screens.title: GPTs·Gems·Skills: Creation structure of three companies
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how the three companies bundle their guidance and materials.

tabs.label: GPTs
tabs.body: ChatGPT's GPTs are created in two ways. In the interactive builder, you describe what you want and ChatGPT creates a draft for you, and in the configuration screen you edit the items yourself. Configuration items are name, description, conversation starter, instructions, knowledge, recommended model, feature, and action. Once created, you can preview it to check tone and accuracy, your changes are saved as a draft, and version history lets you restore previous versions. Business, Enterprise, and Edu workspaces can create and publish GPTs depending on your settings and permissions; personal ChatGPT accounts cannot create or publish new GPTs.

tabs.label: Gems
tabs.body: Gems by Gemini are created by entering a name and instructions. Optionally, you can upload files from Knowledge or import them from Google Drive. The most recent version of the file imported from the drive is used, so any modifications made to the file will be reflected in the Gem. After writing a few words of instructions, you can ask Gemini to rewrite them in more detail, or you can even turn off citing knowledge files. Google Help informs you that Gems will automatically be converted to skills in your personal Google account.

tabs.label: Claude Skills
tabs.body: Claude's skill is a folder containing instructions, executable code, and reference material. It's structured like an onboarding guide for new team members. Claude will automatically use the skill when a relevant request is made. Initially, only the name and description (metadata) of the skill are uploaded to the context, which is the input space read by the model. When the skill is needed, the body instructions are read, and necessary data or code is loaded only when referenced. So, you don't have to repeat the same instructions in every conversation, and the context burden isn't too great even if you have a lot of skills installed.

tabs.label: a moving flow
tabs.body: OpenAI guides you toward moving custom GPTs into plugins. Plugins bundle together reusable instructions, reference files, and connected apps. When moving, the GPT's instructions become skills in the plugin, and the connected app is added as an app in the plugin. After moving, the original GPT becomes read-only, and custom actions are not automatically moved. Google also informs you that Gems in your personal account will be converted to skills. These features are in the transition process, so understanding their structure rather than their names will go a long way.

tabs.label: common structure
tabs.body: All three methods bundle instructions, materials, and tools to be created once and used over and over again. Guidelines dictate how to act, materials provide reference, and tools define the scope of what can be done. Although the name is different, the structure is the same.

screens.outro: So what is different from the project guidelines we saw earlier?

screens.title: Differences between Project Guidelines and Custom Assistants
screens.lead: Tap the switch to compare the scope, sharing methods, and components of your project guidelines and custom assistants.

states.label: Project Guidelines
states.body:
Applies only within one workspace. According to ChatGPT help, project guidelines apply only within that project and take precedence over global custom guidelines. Chat within the project uses the same context, and materials along with instructions are gathered in one place.

Components are instruction- and file-oriented, and are more like settings in a workspace than independent tools with names and descriptions. It provides a space for repetitive tasks and suits the way you work within it.

states.label: custom assistant
states.body:
It is an independent tool with a name and description that can be opened and used by multiple people. No matter who opens it, they start with the same instructions and knowledge, making it ideal for ensuring that everyone on your team uses it in the same way. Editing an instruction or knowledge file will ensure that everyone using it uses the same, up-to-date settings.

There are three components: instructions, knowledge, and tools, and conversation starters guide you through how to use them. How you share depends on your product and workspace settings.

To summarize, a project is a workspace where you work, and a custom assistant is a tool that other people open and use. If it's a task that our entire team repeats, it's easier to manage it if it's in the form of a tool. If you are organizing data that an individual uses alone, a project is sufficient.

screens.outro: Now that you understand the components and their differences, let’s apply them to a real design example.

screens.title: Commentary: Designing a customer inquiry triage assistant
screens.lead: The instructor walks you through the process of designing a customer inquiry triage assistant divided into guidelines, knowledge, and tools. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: Check your work
steps.body: The customer support team categorizes incoming inquiries into “Delivery,” “Refund,” “Technical Support,” and “Other” and informs them of the department in charge every day. Each team member has slightly different classification criteria, so the same inquiry may be classified differently. This task makes for an assistant because it's repetitive, has standards, and requires the entire team to do it the same way.

steps.title: Step 1: Set guidelines
steps.body: Write down the rules and how to answer in the instructions. The key rule is “classify only into one of the following four categories, if ambiguous across two categories don’t classify, ask confirming questions first.” Instead of just listing prohibitions, write with a focus on what needs to be done, and if there are steps, write them down separately in the form of “If this happens, do this.”

steps.title: Step 2: Determine your knowledge
steps.body: References are left to knowledge. Departmental scope of responsibility table and past classification case files are appropriate. These files are not rules, but rather data that the model uses for classification and department guidance. If rules are mixed in knowledge files, it is better to move them into instructions.

steps.title: Step 3: Do you really need the tool?
steps.body: It may seem like you need to search the web or connect to internal systems to find the most up-to-date policies. However, the article advises that problems can often be fixed more quickly if you refine the instructions and add examples before adding tools. This task can be categorized using just the scope table on file, so no additional tools are required.

steps.title: Step 4: Preview and Share
steps.body: Once created, check the tone and accuracy in Preview. We intentionally include vague inquiries and inquiries that span both categories to see if any confirmatory questions arise. After the inspection is completed, share it with the team. If you later change the instructions or knowledge file, the entire team will use the same, up-to-date settings.

screens.outro: Next, we'll look at translating the instructions into actual text.

screens.title: Commentary: Putting Instructions into Words
screens.lead: Below is a translation of the design into actual instruction text. Check the role of each part and the symptoms when it is missing in the explanation next to the code.

data.code:
This assistant classifies customer inquiries and directs them to the appropriate department.

## Classification Rules
1. Classify inquiries into only one of the following: "Shipping", "Refund", "Technical Support", "Other".
2. If ambiguous, do not classify—first ask confirming questions across both categories.
3. After classification, find the responsible department in the scope of knowledge files and inform them.

## Answer Format
- First line: Category
- Second line: Responsible department
- Third line: A portion of the sentence from the inquiry serving as the basis

## Example
Inquiry: "It's been a week since I placed the order, but it hasn't arrived yet."
Response: Shipping / Logistics Team / "It's been a week since the order was placed"

If the responsible department is not listed in the scope of responsibility table, respond with "Responsible department needs to be verified."

notes.note: State the purpose of your assistant in one sentence. If you leave it out, you won't be able to determine what the model is a tool for and may respond with normal conversation.

Classification rule. It is a sentence centered on what needs to be done and even determines what to do in case of ambiguity. If it is omitted, a name outside the category appears or ambiguous inquiries are forced to be classified. Line 6 tells how the rule references material in the knowledge file.
This is the answer format. I decided what to write for each line. If left out, each person will receive a different response format, which undermines the goal of the team writing in the same way.

Here is one example. It helps you understand the format by showing input and expected output in pairs. The help also recommends that when you need to apply classification criteria, you include short examples of acceptable and unacceptable output.
It is a line that specifies actions when the corresponding information is not in the knowledge. If left out, the model may create departments that are not in the scope table.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the contents of this class.

screens.title: Criteria for creating a custom assistant
screens.lead: We will organize the contents so far into the criteria for selecting tasks to create as an assistant.

paragraphs: A custom assistant is a bundle of instructions, knowledge, and tools. Rules and answer methods are placed in instructions, references are placed in knowledge, and the scope of what can be done is placed in tools. Once this distinction is made, version differences and omissions caused by copying prompts disappear, and team members can simply open the assistant and start writing.

Project instructions are written within a single workspace, while custom assistants are independent tools with names and descriptions that can be opened and used by multiple people. If your team is doing things over and over again in the same way, the latter is better.

GPTs are moving to plug-ins and Gems are moving to skills. OpenAI explains that the plugin bundles reusable instructions, reference files, and connected apps, while Google says Gems in your personal account are automatically converted into Skills. Although the names change, the structure of putting together instructions, materials, and tools is the same for all three companies.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Put rules in guidelines and references in knowledge. Add tools only when absolutely necessary, and preview them before sharing.

glossary.def: It is a customized AI that bundles instructions, knowledge, and tools so that everyone can use it in the same way. Representative examples include ChatGPT's GPTs and Gemini's Gems.
These are the rules that determine what your assistant will do, how it will respond, and what it will avoid.
This file is not a rule, but is provided as reference material.
This is a folder containing instructions, code, and reference materials, and is Claude's reusable unit that is automatically used when related requests are made.

misconceptions.myth: Writing rules in a knowledge file is like a guideline.
misconceptions.fact: Knowledge contains reference materials, and help guides you through writing rules, tone, and workflow into instructions. If you mix up roles, rules may not be followed.

misconceptions.myth: The more tools you add, the better.
misconceptions.fact: Problems are often fixed faster if you refine the instructions and add examples before adding tools. Add only the tools you need.

misconceptions.myth: Project guidelines and custom assistants are the same thing.
misconceptions.fact: Project instructions are written within a single workspace, while custom assistants are independent, named tools that can be opened and used by multiple people. The scope of coverage and sharing methods are different.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: A custom assistant is a bundle of instructions, knowledge, and tools.
Keep rules in guidance, references in knowledge, and add tools only when absolutely necessary.
Project instructions are used within the workspace, and custom assistants are used as standalone tools.
GPTs move to plug-ins, Gems move to skills, and the structure of bundling instructions, materials, and tools is the same.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which of our team's recurring tasks would make an assistant?

title: Custom assistants: GPTs, Gems, and instructions

checks.q: What is the appropriate division of roles between guidance and knowledge of a custom assistant?
options: Instructions contain reference materials, and knowledge contains methods of answering.
Instructions contain what to do and how to answer, and knowledge contains uploaded reference materials.
There is no need to differentiate since both have the same role.
Knowledge sets the rules that apply to all conversations
checks.explain: Guidelines determine what to do, how to respond, and what to avoid and apply to all conversations. Knowledge contains data, not rules.

wrong.2: Rules are placed in guidelines, and references are placed in knowledge.
wrong.3: Rules are established by guidelines, not knowledge.

checks.intro: Choose the appropriate option, remembering the role of guidance and knowledge. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: When creating a customer contact triage assistant, what is a good thing to do before adding tools?
options: Turn on both web browsing and external connections first.
Refine the instructions and add examples
Share directly with your team without previewing
checks.explain: The GPTs documentation advises that it is faster to refine the instructions and add examples before adding tools. Before distribution, preview to check tone and accuracy.

wrong.0: Add it after considering whether it is really necessary.
wrong.1: The classification case files are a useful reference.
wrong.3: Check with a preview before sharing.

checks.intro: Think about the design sequence and choose the right option. Results are not recorded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's unfortunate, but other options are better.
